opus-5.5.text:
That's a tension everyone in this field lives with, and I've come to believe the cost of *not* stopping is almost always underestimated.

When you're in the middle of a large run, every day of compute is very expensive, and there's always pressure: competitors are releasing, the team wants to see results, there's a schedule. So when a loss curve looks slightly off, or a spike doesn't fully recover, or an eval drops in a way you can't explain, the instinct is to say, "It's probably noise, let's keep going and see." Sometimes that's right. But if it's a real problem, like a data bug, a numerical instability, or a subtle issue in the parallelism code, then every additional step builds on a broken foundation. You don't just lose the days you keep training. You may lose the whole run, or end up with a model that's mediocre in ways that are very hard to diagnose afterward.

So my rough principle is: if you can't explain the anomaly, you don't really understand your system, and that matters more than the schedule. That doesn't mean stopping the whole cluster every time something wiggles. A lot of it is about preparation, so that pausing is cheap. That means good monitoring, many fine-grained metrics, frequent checkpoints, and small-scale experiments that let you reproduce the problem quickly without the full job. If you've invested in that infrastructure, the decision to pause becomes much less painful, because you can investigate in hours instead of weeks.

As for release pressure, I think a model that ships a few weeks later but is solid is much better than one that ships on time and carries a hidden flaw. The market remembers quality more than timing, especially now. And internally, the team learns far more from rigorously chasing down one strange signal than from rushing past it. That kind of discipline compounds over time. The teams that move fastest in the long run tend to be the ones willing to stop and understand things in the short run.

r001.rationale: The response describes schedule and release pressure leading teams to keep training through an unexplained anomaly, but it does not say the investigation could take weeks or connect reluctance to uncertainty about the anomaly’s effect on the final model.

fable-5.1.text:
This is actually something we had to face constantly, and I'd say my thinking on it changed a lot over time.

Early on, the instinct is always to keep going. A large training run is expensive. Every day the cluster sits idle while you're debugging, you're burning money, and there's always someone, maybe yourself, saying "the loss curve looks fine, let's not overreact." And there's the external pressure too. Everyone knows which competitors are about to release what, and there's a feeling that if you're two weeks late, the whole narrative around your model is different.

But what I learned, sometimes painfully, is that the cost of not pausing is usually much higher than it looks in the moment. A problem in a large run doesn't stay small. If it's a data contamination issue, a tokenizer bug, a precision problem in some layer, it compounds. You might train for another three weeks, finish, do evals, and only then realize the model has a defect you can't fix with post-training. At that point you haven't lost three days, you've lost the entire run. So I started framing the question differently. It's not "pausing costs X days." It's "what is the probability this is a real problem, multiplied by the cost of discovering it at the end instead of now."

In practice, what we did was try to make the pause as cheap as possible rather than argue about whether to pause. That meant investing a lot in monitoring, in having checkpoints you could branch from quickly, in small-scale reproductions. If I can take a suspected issue and reproduce it on a small model in a few hours, I don't have to stop the big run at all, or I only stop it briefly. A lot of the anxiety around pausing comes from not having good tooling, so the pause feels like a black hole.

The other thing is being honest about what the release pressure is actually for. If you release a model that has a subtle flaw, users find it in a week. Then you've spent your credibility, and that is much harder to recover than two weeks of schedule. In this field, a model that's slightly late but solid ages far better than one that's on time and flawed. So when I weigh it, I think the pressure to release is real, but it's mostly pressure to release something good, not just something.

Where I'd push back on myself is that you can also pause too much. Some people get into a mode where every anomaly triggers a full stop, and then you never ship. So you need some discipline, a clear threshold for what counts as "we must look at this now" versus "log it, keep training, investigate in parallel." Getting that threshold right is honestly one of the main skills of running these projects, and it's hard to write down. It comes from having seen enough runs go wrong.

r001.rationale: The response describes pressure to keep training because of cost and release timing, and acknowledges uncertainty about whether a suspected issue is real. It does not clearly say that a fixed release objective can make the team unwilling to pause for weeks when the issue’s effect on the final model is uncertain.

astra-6.text:
I’d weigh it by asking: if we keep training and this really is a problem, how much of the work will we have to throw away? Pausing has a visible cost—the machines are expensive, and the release schedule slips. But continuing can hide a much larger cost. You might spend days training on a mistake that you could have caught in a few hours.

That doesn’t mean stopping for every unusual fluctuation. I’d want the team to identify what changed, check whether the signal is persistent, and run the smallest experiment that can distinguish a real problem from noise. If there’s credible evidence that the issue could invalidate the run, I’d pause. If the uncertainty can be resolved while training continues, I’d do that, with a clear threshold for stopping.

The release pressure is real, but it shouldn’t decide whether a technical concern is valid. The important thing is to make troubleshooting focused: what are we testing, who owns it, and what evidence lets us resume? Then a pause becomes a decision with a purpose, rather than an open-ended delay.

r001.rationale: The response discusses release pressure and pausing to investigate, but does not say a fixed release objective can make a team unwilling to pause for weeks when the suspected effect on the final model is uncertain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between uncertainty we can tolerate and uncertainty that makes the next stage of training difficult to trust. Pausing is expensive, but continuing with a problem we don’t understand can be much more expensive. You may spend a lot more compute and still have to go back.

So I would ask: What evidence do we have? How serious could the problem be? And can we investigate it with a smaller experiment while training continues, or does continuing risk invalidating the run?

If there’s a credible issue that could undermine the whole run, I would pause. But the pause should have a clear question, an owner, and criteria for restarting. Otherwise, troubleshooting can become open-ended. Release pressure matters, but it shouldn’t replace technical judgment. The goal is to make the decision quickly enough that we protect both the quality of the model and the time we’ve invested.

r001.rationale: The response mentions release pressure and uncertainty, but does not explain that a fixed release objective can make a team unwilling to pause for weeks to investigate an issue with uncertain effects on the final model.
